title: The storehouse
hookLine: the storehouse consciousness where the seeds of habit are kept (Lankavatara)

lines: THE SAME WORDS, THE SAME FIGHT.
cards: Why do the same words come out in the same argument, year after year? Nobody sits down at the kitchen table and decides to say them again. They're just there, ready, before anyone has thought anything at all.

The Lankavatara Sutra, and the Yogacara teachers who worked with the same ideas, gave a name to the place where that readiness waits, out of sight. It came up briefly with mind only; today it gets a day of its own.

teach.b: The name is alaya-vijnana, usually translated storehouse consciousness. Yogacara teachers described the mind in layers.

On top, the ones everyone knows: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and the thinking mind that sorts it all out. Under those, a layer that quietly keeps insisting there's a fixed self in charge.
And beneath everything, the storehouse. What's kept there? Seeds; that's the word these teachers used.

Every action, every word, every thought leaves a seed behind. The seed sits there, unseen. Then one day the conditions are right, a certain tone of voice, a certain tired evening, and the seed ripens.
Out comes the reaction, fully formed, as if from nowhere, and that ripening plants new seeds of its own. That's how a habit keeps itself going.
The Lankavatara has a picture for this: the storehouse is like the ocean, and the other kinds of consciousness are like waves, stirred up by the wind of what is seen and heard.
The waves and the ocean are not two separate things. Buddhist schools have argued about this idea. Some worried that a storehouse sounds too much like a hidden, permanent self.
Yogacara teachers answered that it's a stream, never the same from one moment to the next, more like a river than a box. And the teaching runs the other way too.
Seeds can be planted on purpose. A kind word leaves a seed. So does a pause, a breath before answering, one honest apology.
Those seeds also wait in the dark, and they also ripen, sometimes long after anyone remembers planting them.

how: In Yogacara study, and in East Asian and Tibetan schools that inherited it, the storehouse consciousness and its seeds are taught as a way to understand how habits and karma carry forward from moment to moment.

o: the deep layer of mind where seeds of actions wait
the thinking mind that sorts what the senses bring
a monastery building where grain is kept for winter

p: stirred by the wind of what we sense

s: the storehouse is a permanent soul
Yogacara teachers describe it as a stream, never the same from one moment to the next.
in this teaching every action leaves a seed
and when conditions are right, the seed ripens.
only bad habits come from the storehouse
good seeds wait there too: a kind word, a pause, an apology.

games.q: you're a Yogacara teacher, and a student says the storehouse sounds like a hidden, permanent self. what do you answer?
o: it doesn't matter what it is.
games.why: Yogacara teachers answered that the storehouse is a stream, more like a river than a box, never the same from moment to moment.

practice: Sit for a moment and notice how many reactions come up on their own: an itch, a plan, a little worry. Those are seeds ripening; let them pass.
Then picture one small good act, a thank-you or a slower reply, and let the intention sink down like a seed pressed into soil.

wordCard.voice: The storehouse. Alaya-vijnana, the deep layer of mind where, Yogacara teaches, the seeds of every action wait to ripen. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the storehouse consciousness. ālaya, a dwelling or store; vijñāna, consciousness.

carryVoice: Your line: seeds in the storehouse. Some of them were planted on purpose. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Lankavatara Sutra, the ocean-and-waves passage on the alaya-vijnana
